question: Harbourline's first forecast year shows EBIT of £127.2m, depreciation and amortisation of £63.6m, capital expenditure of £70.0m and a £7.2m increase in working capital. Tax is 25 %. What is unlevered free cash flow?
model_answer_md:
Start at EBIT and tax it as though there were no debt:

$$\text{NOPAT} = 127.2 \times (1 - 0.25) = £95.4\text{m}$$

Add back the depreciation and amortisation, because it reduced EBIT without moving any cash, then take out the two real cash costs of running and growing the business:

$$95.4 + 63.6 - 70.0 - 7.2 = \mathbf{£81.8\text{m}}$$

Notice capital expenditure is slightly above D&A here — £70.0m against £63.6m. That is what you expect from a company still growing: it is replacing what wears out and adding a little more.
key_points: Tax EBIT at the full rate — no interest deduction, because this is unlevered
Add back D&A (£63.6m) as a non-cash charge
Subtract capex (£70.0m) and the increase in working capital (£7.2m)

follow_ups.question: What if the company also paid £30m of interest that year?
follow_ups.answer_md: Nothing changes. Unlevered free cash flow is struck before interest by construction — that is the whole point of the word *unlevered*. The £30m does not appear in the cash flow at all; the effect of debt shows up twice elsewhere, in the after-tax cost of debt inside WACC and in the net-debt subtraction on the equity bridge. Deducting it here would double-count the financing.

follow_ups.question: And if D&A were £10m higher, at £73.6m?
follow_ups.answer_md: Two offsetting effects. EBIT falls by £10m to £117.2m, so NOPAT falls by £7.5m to £87.9m — but you add back the full £73.6m rather than £63.6m, which is £10m more. Net effect: **UFCF rises by £2.5m** to £84.3m. That £2.5m is the tax shield, £10m × 25 %. It is the same mechanism as the classic depreciation walkthrough.

weak_answer_note: Deducting interest, or taxing at a rate that reflects the actual interest deduction — both break the 'unlevered' premise. Forgetting the working-capital line, or getting its sign wrong: an *increase* in working capital consumes cash and is subtracted.
